item.title: #MeToo didn’t go far enough
item.description: Can women ever be free from fear?
item.content:encoded:
By Jerusalem Demsas

Once a month, Matt and I do a book club episode of The Argument podcast. In an upcoming episode this month, we are reading Bowling Alone by Robert Putnam. Read along if you are interested, and please comment with any questions or ideas you would like us to explore!

True freedom requires a person with a will — and a society that is organized to allow the expression of that will.

I can want something as simple as to walk my dog at night. But if roving gangs threaten my life, then my freedom to pursue that desire is only theoretical. Even worse is if the threat is so pervasive that I can’t even imagine walking my dog at night. In neither case am I really free.

This diminished freedom has long been, to greater and lesser degrees, the status quo for most women in most places.

Share

Even in a society as egalitarian as the contemporary U.S., polling shows that women feel less safe to roam. Globally, “men are over 20% more likely than women to say they feel safe in their communities.” One paper about women in Delhi finds that women will choose to go to much worse colleges in order to feel safer while traveling, whereas men with similar choices will choose to attend the better colleges more frequently.

One researcher, Alice Evans, recently argued that “our analyses of progress towards gender equality still focus on economic activity and political representation, omitting a far more basic question: can women walk down the street alone at night and be at ease?”

It is not immediately obvious that women should feel less free than men: Men are much more likely than women to be victims of homicide and robbery. Of course, a big part of this is that boys are more likely to be in public spaces unsupervised in the first place.

The freedom to move in the world unburdened by the fear of violence and harassment is a fundamental prerequisite to basically every other freedom we care about: to say what you really think, to associate with whomever you wish. It can be hard to imagine a world where the average woman remains physically weaker than the average man and yet feels as free. But one thing gives me hope: If you were to describe the freedom enjoyed by many women in rich, low-crime neighborhoods in modern-day America to a woman living in the 1700s, it would become clear just how much legal, social, and cultural progress can be made.

#MeToo’s unfinished revolution

The slogan Me Too was first used in 2006 by the activist Tarana Burke to promote what she called “empowerment through empathy.” The idea was that victims of sexual violence and harassment often feel isolated by their experiences. Making people aware that there are others who have gone through the same thing plausibly makes them feel less alone.

But after the hashtag went truly viral in 2017, the slogan’s original purpose no longer seemed to meet the enormity of the task. The allegations against Harvey Weinstein and other abusive male power brokers were horrifying, and the veritable downpour of crimes revealed by women everywhere felt endless. We couldn’t wait for the broad social awareness being cultivated by the hashtag to trickle down into people’s behavior. Responding to stories of assault, harassment, and inequality with mere “likes” on social media was clearly not enough.

But the signal failure of #MeToo was that in seeking to counteract the norm of doubting women’s accounts, “accused” became nearly synonymous with “guilty.” More broadly, #MeToo, by highlighting women’s vulnerability, cast all men in the role of perpetrator.

Subscribe now

In 2022, Burke wrote a retrospective in which she gave examples of the accomplishments of #MeToo. Besides removing “captains of industry” from positions of power, her examples were largely expressive:

  • “More than any law that has been passed or policy that has been changed in the past five years, this movement has created visibility and community.”

  • “The language we use is shifting, replacing words like victim with survivor.”

  • “We talk about mental health and healing.”

  • “[E]mployers are crafting thoughtful human-resource policies.”

  • “Consumers are more conscientious about the cultural content they consume.”

  • Consumers are “vocal about calling out rape culture.”

Burke, not totally comfortable with this accounting, quoted another feminist author, Imani Perry, who argued that “awareness is not a virtue in and of itself.” Burke expressed ambivalence about incarcerating more rapists and ended her piece by calling on the reader to do their part.

But what is their part? If awareness is not enough, and the goal is to effect mass cultural change without incarcerating a lot more rapists, what exactly should we be doing?

My cohost Matt Yglesias argued that the #MeToo movement was thin on specific demands and failed to accomplish very much, which is reasonable enough. Earlier feminist wins were concrete: Recognize our right to vote. Recognize our right to own property. Recognize our right to divorce our husbands and attend college.

The main problem is that both critics and supporters of the #MeToo movement tended to underrate just how radically society would have to change for women to feel as safe as men, or even to come close.

For starters, there is no specific legislative demand that could eliminate sexual harassment. And sexual violence is different from other serious crimes like murder or theft. There is often not dispositive physical evidence like there would be if someone shot you or broke into your house, and therefore cases are typically based almost entirely on witness testimony.

Moreover, victims themselves are often torn about going through the legal system. Sometimes they just want to move on rather than deal with a years-long process that may retraumatize them while hinging entirely on their perceived credibility as a witness. Sometimes the perpetrator is a friend, partner, or community member who they don’t actually want sent to jail.

And, of course, so much of what makes women and girls feel unsafe is not rape itself but the threat of sexual harassment that does not rise to the level of criminal activity.

True equality for women cannot exist in a world where girls are afraid to walk home from school alone and women have to remain on high alert while going about their normal lives. The unfortunate fact is that you can’t legislate freedom.

You can’t bar men from catcalling 13-year-olds, or from leering at women jogging at night. So, what do you do? I don’t think there’s an obvious answer.

item.title: Pigs vs. democracy
item.content:encoded:
By John Robert Thomason

Welcome to The Closing Argument, our verdict on the news, plus everything The Argument published and appeared in this week.

The Verdict, by John Thomason

Americans, we keep learning, are obsessed with the price of groceries. At the same time, many of them seem very uncomfortable with one of the ways that meat producers make groceries cheap: by cramming livestock so close together that they can’t even turn around.

When you pose this problem to voters a kind of commonsense decency can sometimes win out: Healthy majorities in Florida, Arizona, Massachusetts, and California have voted in favor of raising confinement standards over the last 25 years.

You might notice that none of those are major pork-producing states.

But because the initiatives in California and Massachusetts limited not just what their farmers could do, but also what sorts of animal products could be sold within their borders at all, the animal welfare implications were immense, amounting to perhaps the most substantial protections for farmed animals in U.S. history. The 2018 passage of California’s Proposition 12 meant that, if hog farmers in Iowa want to sell whole cuts of pork to Californians (which they very much do), they have to abide by Golden State standards.

All of that was almost thrown out over the course of this spring and summer.

The Farm Bill is a sprawling document that covers everything from food stamps to irrigation programs — an ideal vehicle for a policy change to escape public notice. That seems to be at least in part what the proponents of the Save Our Bacon Act were hoping for. The provision, championed by members of Iowa’s congressional delegation, would have preempted state-level reforms like California’s and Massachusetts’s, making it impossible for states to bar the sale of pork from pigs whose mothers couldn’t turn around or extend their limbs during pregnancy (so long as those farms’ states allow it).

Farm-state Republicans lined up behind the provision, while food safety groups, animal rights groups, and most of the Democratic Senate caucus were against it. (The pork industry is actually split between those who have not yet complied with strict standards and those who have already invested in compliant practices.) The latter appeared to be winning out in June, when the Senate decided not to include the provision, apparently over the controversy it had engendered. But that doesn’t mean Save Our Bacon is dead. The Farm Bill stalled in the Senate Agriculture Committee on Thursday, over a dispute on an entirely different issue, with the committee now in recess until the fall. The Save Our Bacon Act is likely to get a second wind at that time.

If we’re being honest, the vast majority of the nation didn’t just miss this drama — they probably wouldn’t have cared all that much if they’d known.

It’s common to hear political junkies talk about “high salience” and “low salience” issues. The cost of pork is high salience — something voters will definitely notice and express their dissatisfaction about at the polls — while the welfare of the pigs who suffered to keep prices down is low salience, the purview largely of those who in some sense have made a choice to care about it.

With high salience issues, the will of the voters is clear enough and the cost of ignoring it is losing elections. But on low salience issues, democracies count on elite political actors reaching some sort of reasonable agreement that is in the best interests of the public.

The conflict over Save Our Bacon unsettles the idea that low and high salience issues are cleanly separable.

First of all, which “will of the voters” should be honored in this situation? That of the median 2024 voter, angry about the price of groceries, or those of the actual majorities in multiple states who voted for farm animal protections? (Even Iowa voters appear to reject the Save Our Bacon Act, though the poll in question was commissioned by an advocacy organization.)

Still, asking people to improve pigs’ lives is one thing; asking them to pay a lot more for bacon, let alone give it up entirely, is another. Ending farm animal suffering would require the latter. If animal rights become high salience, animal rights groups lose. If it stays low salience, then they never even get a shot at winning. Such is the fate of those with unpopular convictions in a democratic society.

No country for moral fanatics?

Four years ago, a very small dog wandered into my life, and it changed my politics forever.

I had always been a little judgy about people who dote on their pets, yet there I was, realizing that I might find myself in tears if this ornery creature had so much as a hangnail. It no longer made sense to me to care so much about the welfare of this one animal without caring about others who seemed just like him.

Most market hogs are mutilated without anesthesia, spend their lives on bare slats above their own manure, and never go outdoors until slaughter. If we did any of this to dogs we’d call it torture. None of this was exactly news to me, I’m ashamed to say, but for the first time I actually felt that it might be impossible to live with myself if I knew that, while I doted on this dog, creatures just like him were being put through hell on earth for me.

In a political climate where we’re constantly being told that the moral stakes are higher than ever — that, as former President Obama lamented in 2015, “those who disagree with us are not merely wrong but bad” — contemplating the fate of livestock induces a kind of vertiginous loneliness, precisely because it’s not a matter of public controversy. Quite the opposite: Per-capita meat consumption has never been higher, and all either party can talk about is making that consumption cheaper. Meanwhile, more than 80 billion farm animals are slaughtered worldwide every year after the sort of lives I described above.

But different people have dramatically different moral red lines. Many of my fellow citizens think that we’re living through a genocide of unborn children. Others think that we should strip private property rights from anyone with one too many 0’s in their net worth. I don’t agree with either of them, and most of them don’t agree with me. We have to live together anyway. A certain amount of moral loneliness — the kind that could keep you up at night, aghast at the evil that people will tolerate — is the price that every zealot pays to live in a democratic society. At least I know they won’t hang me for it.

It’s uncomfortable to realize you’re part of a moral minority. What options do you have, besides the despair of accepting majority will, or the tireless fanaticism that characterizes groups like PETA?

It’s here that I take some solace in the weird indeterminacy of representative democracy. If you put the actual question I care about before voters — would you give up meat as you know it to end farm animal suffering? — it would lose. If you put the question purely to elite power brokers, it would also lose.

In a majoritarian society, moral minorities will never be entirely satisfied. Ninety-nine percent of the time this brings me great relief: I don’t want anti-abortion zealots dictating health policy by fiat. Yet I too believe that egregious moral crimes are being committed daily and, yes, I would impose my preference for stopping these crimes on everyone else if I could. If only I could.

But of course I don’t want to be imposed upon myself. For all its backsliding, the American system still does a pretty good job of ensuring that. And the very fragmentation that helps shore up this freedom — the separation of powers, the strategic veto points, the uneasy coalitions — also gives radicals of every stripe avenues to pursue their goals. It’s not such a lonely place for a fanatic after all.

Top stories this week, by Milan Singh

Starting off the week, Kobe Yank-Jacobs wrote about the popularity of different AI labs in The Argument’s polling. OpenAI is the most popular lab — even among regular AI users and those especially concerned about existential risk.

For the first time ever, more people are employed by remodeling companies than by single-family and multifamily developers combined. Economics writer Joey Politano highlighted the surge in home renovations: Rather than building new units, Americans are increasingly renovating existing homes. Unfortunately, renovations alone aren’t enough to fix our housing supply problems.

Have you ever seen a 2-year-old learn the commutative property of addition? Staff writer Kelsey Piper, who recently welcomed her fourth child, explains how certain aspects of modernity have made parenting harder, even as life has gotten better. Come for the precocious 2-year-old; stay for the meditation on Baumol’s cost disease.

🌟Abundance wins of the week🌟

  • The feds closed a $489 million loan to add 220 megawatts of batteries to Puerto Rico’s grid, capable of providing backup electricity to more than 100,000 customers during shortages, thus avoiding millions of customer interruption hours. Puerto Rico’s notoriously unreliable grid certainly needs it!

  • Wayne County, Michigan, is doing state-capacity praxis. On Tuesday, a supermajority of voters approved a plan to bring 17 previously opted-out communities into the single countywide system, filling longstanding gaps in the region’s public transportation network.

  • Because of Texas’ new statewide preemption, the Nacogdoches City Council unanimously changed its zoning code. HUD-code manufactured homes, for the first time in over 20 years, will be buildable by right in a residential zoning district.

Share

Worth watching…

This week on the podcast, Matt and Jerusalem discussed the #MeToo movement. Jerusalem thinks it didn’t go far enough, a somewhat troll-y way of saying that the work of feminism is not yet finished. Matt strikes a more skeptical tone, arguing that the movement lacked a clear set of policy “asks,” which makes it difficult to even evaluate its successes.

Lakshya Jain and VoteHub’s Zachary Donnini discussed counting mail-in ballots with Nevada Secretary of State Cisco Aguilar. You can’t run elections cheaply, accurately, and quickly, Aguilar said; you have to pick two of the three. If you’ve ever wondered why California takes so long to count votes, this is for you.

Kobe Yank-Jacobs went live with JS Denain, a senior researcher at Epoch AI, to discuss recursive self-improvement (RSI). The big labs are very bullish on RSI’s ability to speed up the pace of AI development, but Denain argued that AI’s potential to actually make useful research contributions is more limited than boosters let on.

What’s News with The Argument

The Argument recommends, by Milan Singh

Both Editor-in-Chief Jerusalem Demsas and Staff Writer Kelsey Piper recommend you pick up A Trade of Blood, the recently released third book in Robert Jackson Bennett’s fantasy series.

“For those who haven’t read it, the first book, The Tainted Cup, is a fantastic book about the murder of an imperial officer that is part Sherlockian mystery and part meditation on the running of an empire,” Jerusalem explained.

“I think the murder mystery format is weirdly well suited to the meditations on empire,” added Kelsey. “If you read British mystery novelists (Doyle, Christie, Heyer, le Carré) you can kind of watch the empire exhaust its case for itself and collapse in the background, and Bennett is clearly wrestling with American empire — notwithstanding the extremely wild biopunk sci-fi setting.”

Senior Editor John Thomason has been listening to Don DeLillo’s White Noise while commuting into the office: “Something about the folksy narration — from veteran stage actor Michael Prichard, who grew up on a farm himself and absolutely nails the chapter on the most photographed barn in America — is making me see DeLillo’s novel less as the landmark of postmodern lit that I remember from college and instead as surprisingly faithful to the 19th-century realist tradition, or maybe a kind of pastoral.”

Gender and culture writing fellow Maibritt Henkel watched the millennial classic 13 Going on 30: “While it is a very silly movie, I would say two things in my defense: (1) it belongs to Mark Ruffalo’s complete works and should therefore be considered part of the cinematic canon, and (2) considering your life and your morals from the perspective of your 13-year-old self is a pretty profound exercise.”

Editor Eli Richman has been going back and forth between reading the Dungeon Crawler Carl books and watching the new season of House of the Dragon. “I worry [House of the Dragon] is catching The Boys syndrome, where the need to have things go badly for the protagonists overwhelms the need for the story to make sense,” he said. “Dungeon Crawler Carl is unironically fantastic, ping-ponging between absurdly silly and very real without missing a beat.”

Finally, I personally do not recommend being hit by a car. The adrenaline rush is something else, but it hurts quite a bit.

item.title: I don’t need you to believe I’m a woman
item.description: The important thing is that you believe in my rights
item.content:encoded:
By Cassie Pritchard

Editor’s note: The first essay The Argument ever published asked, “How do we live with each other?” To mark our first anniversary on August 17, we’re returning to that founding question with a series about what we owe people whose beliefs and choices we may find difficult to accept or even understand. Over the next six weeks, familiar voices at The Argument and new voices alike will approach that question from different angles.

Cassie Pritchard opens the series by confronting the painful reality that many of the people with whom she shares a country will never believe she is a woman. Rather than seek their affirmation, Pritchard demands something less intimate and more important: That they defend her freedom and security anyway.

To receive every essay in this series, subscribe today.

- Jerusalem Demsas

I don’t think of myself as a particularly respectable trans woman.

I didn’t start taking hormones until I was 30; I’m a lesbian; I don’t pass as cis female, nor do I make much effort to modulate my voice to sound more feminine. Not to put too fine a point on it, but I’m also kind of weird-looking. Conventional beauty is the single biggest weapon in a trans woman’s arsenal for assimilation and respect, and I’m decidedly outgunned in most situations.

I say all of this to explain why I find it so odd that other trans people regularly criticize me for promoting “respectability politics.” Their assumption seems to be that I’m one of the small handful of trans people who disagree with the premise that trans people actually are our transitioned sex. But I do not. Indeed, I can’t really imagine why someone would bother going through hormone therapy, hair removal, and difficult surgery recoveries if they didn’t think all that work resulted in a genuine and thoroughgoing transformation.

The core of my contention is that we need to move away from airy, philosophical debates about the ontology of sex and gender and instead ground our advocacy in common values and clear moral narratives. After years of slogans like “trans women are women” functioning as progressive shibboleths — so rarely explained, so rarely justified through persuasion — it’s time to sideline them from our mass politics. That would mean fewer condescending explainer videos about what gender really is and more straightforward appeals to individual liberty, pluralism, tolerance, care for the disenfranchised, and parents’ rights to make medical decisions for their children (including the right to choose youth gender medicine!).

Share

I am not interested in policing what cis people think about me. Many think of me as a man. Others think of me as some strange liminal creature between male and female, a “secret third thing,” as the meme goes. A few (I tend to believe very few, but I’m a bit pessimistic by nature) genuinely think of me as a woman, and that’s lovely! I prioritize those people as friends or partners, as human beings generally seek out those who validate our self-conception, who respect our capacity for self-realization.

That said, what makes for a good social life and secure friendships is not necessarily what builds the kind of popular coalitions needed to secure political and material rights, like access to health care. Pro-trans positions have taken a beating over the last decade. For example, while Pew Research Center found that majorities of Americans opposed bathroom bans in 2016, recent polling has found a complete reversal, with majorities of American voters supporting these restrictions: A February poll from The Argument showed 52% of respondents supporting such bans. I can’t help but think that part of the explanation for this whipsaw in public opinion is that we have built a pro-trans advocacy movement too interested in disciplining thoughts and words — and Americans really dislike a scold.

It’s not just bathroom policing where we’ve lost ground. Even bigger majorities were in favor of banning youth gender medicine and barring trans youth from competing on K-12 sports teams that conform to their transitioned sex.

These majorities reject trans-specific policies that are dependent on a firm belief that trans people like me are our transitioned sex. Sports is a good example: If you believe trans girls are girls, then even if they possessed a generalized advantage over cis girls, excluding them would make no sense. That axis of difference would be orthogonal to the “girls’ sports” classification giving them the right to compete — it would be like forcing especially tall girls to play basketball on boys teams as a remedy for their innate advantage over shorter players.

To put it more bluntly, I see the majority who oppose sports inclusion as a kind of minimum percentage of Americans who reject the ontological premise of transition — that we really are, or can become, the gender we transition into.

Many trans people find this incredibly bleak or downright hopeless. Because we have so thoroughly premised our claims to rights and inclusion on the logic that “trans men are men, trans women are women,” it can feel like an irrevocable defeat to even acknowledge that large majorities of cis people disagree with our beliefs about the nature of sex and gender.

But the same poll from The Argument also found 63% of voters in favor of laws to protect trans people from housing and job discrimination. Other polls have delivered essentially the same result: Majorities of Americans still support classic, familiar civil rights protections for trans people that closely mirror the rights won by other minority groups through persuasive political struggle.

These strong pro-civil-rights majorities point to the way forward: It’s not merely that we can secure some protections while giving up our (presently) losing issues as lost causes. Almost the entire pro-trans platform can be defended in the moral language of civil rights and American pluralism, rather than via the epistemics of gender identity.

Subscribe now

As an example, letting me use the women’s bathroom doesn’t have to be premised on your agreeing with (or politely humoring) my self-conception. Instead, you might oppose bathroom bans because the enforcement regimes are necessarily open to abuse by busybodies and delusional conspiracists who think hordes of cis people are secretly trans.

Do you really want to get arrested because a crazy person accused you of being in the wrong bathroom at the airport? Sure, you can prove your natal sex in the end, but in the meantime, you’ve had to endure a humiliating, invasive, and stupid ordeal to get there — and missed your flight in the process.

Such an argument is classically American, in my view: against intrusive government overreach and in favor of sharing public space with people we may not agree with, like, or feel kinship with. The freedom to pee in whatever bathroom you want may seem trivial compared to free speech or religious practice, but, like so many freedoms, curtailing it requires a distinctly un-American apparatus of mutual surveillance, control, and nuisance.

It’s the kind of busybody policymaking that might jibe with, say, the English nanny state, but not here in the land of the free.

These are urgent questions because trans people face real material insecurity: We are about five times more likely to be unemployed than the general population, we make substantially less money when we are employed, we face housing discrimination, and we face concerning levels of violence. Maybe most distressingly of all, the president and his party are assailing us with a wave of punitive policies, including barring us from the military and attempting to restrict youth gender medicine. Though the administration has suffered setbacks on the latter, 27 states currently restrict youth gender medicine.

These very real threats make it essential to have coalitional arguments that foreground civil rights if we want to restore public support for pro-trans policy. This can benefit both trans people and a left-of-center coalition anxious about how our rights might be an electoral drag.

I analogize it to the bedrock American principle of religious freedom: Most Muslim or Mormon Americans don’t premise their rights and dignity on everyone necessarily sharing their religious convictions, but on a mutual ethic of noninterference and nondiscrimination. If trans people can make the same kinds of arguments — that we have a common interest in mutual respect despite different beliefs about gender — we stand a chance at rebuilding the coalitions we need for our security.

Respectability without respect

Still, my opening question remains: Why, exactly, do my beliefs about effective political communication so regularly draw this accusation of “respectability politics”?

The logic of respectability politics is that, by assimilating to hegemonic cultural norms, the minority group in question will be seen less as a threatening and deviant “other” and instead as a harmless, superficially distinct extension of the mainstream. The term was coined by historian Evelyn Brooks Higginbotham to describe efforts to “reform ... individual behavior and attitudes both as a goal in itself and as a strategy for the reform of the entire structural system.”

Classically, this has meant things like Cosby-style advice to young Black men to pull up their pants, efforts to use “correct” English in place of Black vernacular, and so on. In the LGBT rights context, it has generally meant publicly sidelining behaviors like cruising and orgies in favor of the respectable image of two gay people in a monogamous marriage raising children in a house with a white picket fence.

But here’s the thing: I like lesbian orgies, my sex-worker friends, and my natural baritone voice that juxtaposes strangely (for most people) with my 540 cc breast implants. I long ago realized that passing as a cis woman was not possible for me — and I wasn’t willing to put in the work even if it were. I’m trans, I’m odd, and I don’t have much interest in hiding either fact.

The “respectability politics” accusation is all the more confusing because, to my mind, requiring cis people to agree that “trans women are women” seems precisely to be a demand for respect — in this case, a respect for the ontological status of our transitioned sex. Doing that while decrying respectability politics — the effort to secure the majority’s respect by appealing to its normative sensibilities — is an incoherent position.

The position of my accusers seems to be that the majority’s respect is politically essential, that we need to secure it as the foundation of our political advancement. But the very same people argue that we have a moral duty to eschew any effort to actually cultivate that respect by appealing to majority sensibilities.

It’s the solicitousness of respectability politics without any of the practical upside. We might call this degenerated form of respectability politics “respect me!” politics instead.

Anyone who has spent time in progressive or leftist circles is immediately familiar with this dynamic: an unyielding commitment to rhetorical hostility coupled with a demand for affection from the very people they’re attacking. There seems to be a belief that respect, affinity, or solidarity can be enforced through disciplinary measures like shaming, belittling, and ostracism.

Subscribe now

While, mercifully, this rhetorical strategy seems to be on the decline on the broader left (perhaps best exemplified by Zohran Mamdani’s refrain that we need to “[go] from lecturing to listening”), it remains alarmingly pervasive on trans issues. This was particularly evident in the online reaction to The Argument’s February poll.

The survey simply reported the dire facts about public opinion on trans issues, yet it resulted in a wave of backlash in which commenters accused Lakshya Jain, The Argument’s director of political data, of “preemptive surrender” and “suggesting Dems abandon trans rights.” One of the top Twitter responses captured the anti-democratic implications succinctly: “fuck whatever a poll says.”

Whenever I make the case to other trans people that we need to stop making demands on cis people’s feelings, beliefs, and speech — and instead appeal to common principles like liberty and equality — I am met with choruses asking me, incredulously, “Where’s your self-respect?” This further complicates the picture; it seems that self-respect is curiously tied up in the active antagonism of the majority.

On the one hand, the insistence on securing cis people’s respect for our gender identities betokens a kind of insecure, almost conservative premise shared by classic respectability politics. On the other hand, those committed to antagonism recognize that there’s something a bit beggarly in this premise, something self-consciously weak.

Instead of reconciling the tension between these two urges — for self-respect and pride on one side, and longing for the majority’s normative respect on the other — by simply choosing one and following through, “respect me!” politics amalgamates both into a miserable chimera. The resulting creature craves approval but loathes the prostration required to secure it; instead, approval is demanded but never obtained, because you can’t actually browbeat people into liking or respecting you. It is a self-defeating urge, simultaneously haughty and insecure.

The way I choose to resolve this problem is not by denying its existence or capitulating to it. Instead, it is precisely because I believe trans people are not generally respected as our transitioned sex that I believe we must shift to an argument for our rights and safety premised on moral narratives and values that sit apart from that question entirely.

You do not need to believe I really am a woman to think I deserve protection from employment or housing discrimination. You don’t need to believe people really can change their sex to think that trans people deserve access to the primary kind of medical care that resolves the empirically documented harms of gender dysphoria. You do not need to think gender is a spectrum to think that parents and doctors — and not the government — should be making health care decisions for their children.

I’m willing to be part of a coalition where many people do not believe the things I believe about transsexuality and gender. I’m not thrilled about it, and it’s often dispiriting. But I am willing to tolerate those beliefs, even when they’re uncomfortable or painful, for the sake of obtaining our freedoms and material security.

Without improving trans people’s actual security, I don’t think we’ll ever arrive at the kind of social acceptance that will eliminate the insecurities at the heart of “respect me!” politics.

By Jerusalem Demsas

Next week marks one year since The Argument was born. The very first thing we published was an essay of mine called “How do we live with each other?“ It asked the question at the heart of this magazine.

Well-meaning people disagree profoundly on the best way to live. Some of them think you should get married and have children by 22. Others think religion is a poison. Still others believe that eating a hamburger is a grave sin.

These people are often illegible to one another.

So how do we build a society together amid all that disagreement? That is the work of liberalism and is therefore the work of The Argument.

To mark our first anniversary, we’re returning to that founding question with a series about what we owe people whose beliefs and choices we may find difficult to accept or even understand.

Our first piece in this series came out today. In “I don’t need you to believe I’m a woman,” Cassie Pritchard argued that trans rights cannot depend on persuading everyone to share the same beliefs about gender.

item.title: Does it really matter that we're bowling alone?
item.description: A skeptical debate on social capital
item.content:encoded:
By Jerusalem Demsas

“What prepares men for totalitarian domination in the non-totalitarian world is the fact that loneliness, once a borderline experience usually suffered in certain marginal social conditions like old age, has become an everyday experience of the evergrowing masses of our century.”

Hannah Arendt wrote those words in the 1950s, but concern that modern life has become unbearably lonely has reached a fever pitch in recent years. Basically everyone I know and respect (and many I do not) is worried about a crisis of community driven by individual isolation. The generalized concern draws together several otherwise distinct anxieties about modern American life:

  • Kids aren’t partying enough or drinking enough or having enough premarital sex.

  • We spend so much time on our phones and not enough time hanging out with our friends.

  • Nobody knows their neighbors.

  • A decline in social trust seems to be making our politics unbelievably toxic.

I have a knee-jerk aversion to declensionist narratives, so the widespread gloom about an alleged death spiral in American community life makes me suspicious. To begin exploring whether I’m too Pollyannaish about the decline of formal bowling leagues, my co-host Matt Yglesias and I decided to read Bowling Alone (2000) by Robert Putnam.

Putnam’s book argues that American associational life has collapsed dramatically as highly civic older cohorts have died off. There’s very little in the book about bowling leagues per se, but Putnam documents how religious organizations, unions, Rotary clubs, and local organizations of all types have seen their membership fall. Younger cohorts have eschewed the joiner-ism of their parents and grandparents.

The causes of this decline are hotly debated. Putnam largely blames it on generational replacement but also points to TV and suburbanization, among other factors.

Bowling Alone is fixated on the idea of social capital — that associational life is the way that communities build social networks and norms of reciprocity and trustworthiness. As a result, if people aren’t joining bowling leagues anymore, they’re slowly squandering the collective bank of social capital, with dire consequences for all.

I think it’s trivially obvious to point out that people are spending more time alone. Being alone is a lot easier and more fun than it used to be.

But the leap people take from that fact to speculating about mass loneliness and disconnection, the end of democracy and liberalism, and generalized unhealthiness seems half-baked to me. Being alone, feeling lonely, and lacking social capital are related but distinct conditions.

Share

Recent polling from The Argument showed that very few people identify as a lonely person, which directionally supported findings from Pew Research Center that 47% of people say they hardly ever or never feel lonely or isolated. Just 16% say they feel lonely or isolated all or most of the time.

Even if traditional associational social capital has declined, many of the valuable outcomes Putnam attributes to it seem to have survived through other mechanisms. One moving anecdote from early in the book recounts a man donating his kidney to another participant in his bowling league in Ypsilanti, Michigan. Putnam tells this story to illustrate the value of social capital, but that raises the question: Are there fewer people donating kidneys now? No. In 1997, there were 11,701 donations (3,927 from living donors) and in 2025 there were 27,573 (6,521 from living donors).

Other outcomes Putnam points to like crime, dropout rates, teen pregnancies, and premature deaths among children have changed — largely for the better — in the 26 years since he published his book. And it did not take a widespread revival in associational life. At the end of the 544 pages, I was honestly unable to identify a clear reason why I should care about associational life.

Subscribe now

Putnam, like many people worried about social disconnection and the decline of community life, hopes that politics will save us. Throughout the book, he points to increasing political participation as the path forward.

Well, 26 years later and we certainly appear to have a lot more people talking about, thinking about, and working in politics! Has that revived America’s community spirit? You be the judge.

Matt thinks I’m too harsh on Putnam — who correctly understood the threat that watching TV all the time would continue to isolate us — but agrees that some of his prescriptions are wrongheaded.

item.title: The Michigan senate race is Abdul El-Sayed’s to lose
item.description: Our model shows Abdul El-Sayed can survive a "squad"-level underperformance
item.content:encoded:
By Lakshya Jain

The Split Ticket midterms model is updated daily at 5 p.m. Eastern with the latest polls on our website.

We’ve seen a lot of cases where swing-state Republicans nominate ardently ideological, base-aligned candidates over more “establishment” options. Abdul El-Sayed’s primary victory may be the first instance in modern memory where Democrats have done the same in a critical statewide race.

Primary voters are not reflective of the general electorate, and many of those Republicans lost winnable races as a result. But there’s reason to believe El-Sayed’s fate could be different.

There are real risks associated with his candidacy: Our Split Ticket midterms model sees him as a slightly weaker candidate than his primary opponent Rep. Haley Stevens would have been. Stevens had an 80% chance of winning the general election, according to the model, while El-Sayed’s odds are currently at 70%. While we estimate that Stevens would have won by 5.4 percentage points, we think El-Sayed will win by just 3.6 points, thanks to his substantially weaker polling.

Share

Why is El-Sayed still forecast to win, despite his relative weakness? The single biggest reason is a national and state environment that’s uniquely unfriendly to Republicans.

In 2024, when Donald Trump won the popular vote by 1.5 percentage points nationally, Michigan was an R+1 state. Today, that number is closer to D+9 by our estimation (or D+8, if you look at Nate Silver’s modeling). In that sort of environment, even if El-Sayed’s candidate quality is similar to that of the average hardline progressive from “The Squad” (meaning he would perform 5 points worse than a replacement-level Democrat), he would still win.

Are national polls simply wrong about how blue 2026 might be? I don’t think so. Every other indication we’re seeing, ranging from special elections to the Washington state jungle primary, suggests that this really is a blue tsunami of a cycle.1 And in a situation like that, El-Sayed doesn’t need to overperform or even match the baseline performance of generic Democrats. He simply needs to avoid being a disaster.

Can he do that? It’s early, but I’d say the initial signs are promising. He has distanced himself from controversial remarks about 9/11 by Hasan Piker, who campaigned with him. He appears to be embracing party unity and has disavowed his own prior left-wing comments on defunding the police.

In doing so, El-Sayed appears to be avoiding many of the same missteps that plagued Republican firebrands like 2022 Arizona gubernatorial candidate Kari Lake. Also working in El-Sayed’s favor is the fact that Republican nominee Rep. Mike Rogers has made absolutely no effort to distance himself from Trump, flirting with election denial despite running in a state where the president is supremely unpopular.2

That’s why, if you forced me to pick today, I’d say that El-Sayed still wins this race.

Our model is more bullish on El-Sayed than other quantitative forecasts,3 in part because we don’t pay as much attention to pre-primary polling,4 and in part because our generic ballot modeling of Michigan suggests El-Sayed would have to underperform at the level of Elizabeth Warren (who underperformed by 11 points in her last Senate race) in order to lose.

This means he’d have to be nearly twice as weak as the average member of “The Squad,” for whom the typical underperformance is 5 points. While there’s plenty of evidence to suggest El-Sayed is weaker than Stevens would have been, there’s simply no evidence to support the hypothesis he’s that much weaker than a replacement-level Democrat.

This has implications for 2028 as well. Because while election nerds like me will look at overperformance and evaluate whether a win was by “more” or “less” than expected, that’s just not how the median voter looks at things. For a party whose left flank is ascendant, any win from El-Sayed is likely to be held up as proof that their candidates can actually win swing states — and probably gives fuel to the left in the 2028 presidential primaries.

For a long time, candidates like El-Sayed were simply boxed out of Democratic primaries — for anything other than safely blue races — due to concerns about electability as well as struggles with nonwhite segments of the party base. It was this phenomenon that tanked both Warren and Bernie Sanders in the 2020 presidential primary. And if the primary between Stevens and El-Sayed had been held in 2020, it is virtually certain that Stevens — who lost by just 1 percentage point this time — would have won.

But amid the historic unpopularity of both Trump and the Democratic establishment — and in the context of the never-ending conflict in Gaza, which dominated this primary — it is clear that 2026 is a different landscape altogether. Rank-and-file Democrats may well see El-Sayed’s nomination as a relevant test of the left’s ability to win swing states.

Whether that’s true or not, it could have seismic implications for the direction Democrats choose to go in 2028.

item.title: Men also want it all
item.content:encoded:
By Maibritt Henkel

Men are no longer the breadwinners they once were. In 1972, husbands earned more than their wives in at least 85% of American marriages. Husbands were the sole earners in more than half of those.

Today, the share of heterosexual married couples where the man makes more money than the woman has fallen to just 55%. Only 23% of marriages rely solely on a husband’s income. And it’s not just women’s earning potential that has increased their economic independence: Unlike most of their midcentury counterparts, women today can open credit card accounts and take out mortgages without the bank requiring a man’s sign-off.

Some see the rise of the female breadwinner as a bad deal for men. Women may have gained independence, but they have done so at the cost of men’s sense of purpose. “Men are more likely to flourish when they see themselves as providers,” wrote Brad Wilcox, a University of Virginia professor and author of the book Get Married: Why Americans Must Defy the Elites, Forge Strong Families, and Save Civilization, along with co-author Maria Baer. “Men do better when they feel needed — and being a reliable breadwinner makes them feel needed.”

But The Argument’s latest poll of 3,000 registered voters, fielded nationally between July 20 and 26, suggests that an end to male breadwinning might actually suit men’s preferences just fine.

When asked whether they personally agreed or disagreed with the statement “men should be the breadwinner,” just 34% of all male respondents agreed. A substantial majority disagreed.

Share

One explanation for what is going on here is that men are answering out of solidarity with women — or, more cynically, a desire to give the socially desirable response — rather than pure self-interest. They reject the traditional division of labor into male breadwinning and female caregiving because they understand that sharing these responsibilities is good for women.

And yet, when we asked men what was more important to them — career success or getting married and having children — 44% of men prioritized family while 41% prioritized work, around the same shares as women. Among conservative men, the share prioritizing getting married and having children was even higher.

On the right, there is a sense that feminism has forced men into egalitarian relationships they do not want. Traditional marriage gave men a clearly defined role: to provide the primary income to their families. They would like that script back because without it they are in crisis.

Conversely, the left has tended to frame men relinquishing the breadwinner role as a moral imperative. There’s a sense that cheering on their wives’ careers and taking on child care is the least they can do.

Neither framing captures what our polling indicates: that changing gender norms around who spends time at home and who spends time at work might actually align with men’s own interests. Indeed, a majority of fathers say they spend too little time with their children, mostly due to work obligations.

Men don’t know what other men want

The idea that most men want to be breadwinners is not just culturally pervasive — it’s what the men we surveyed think, too. Despite a plurality prioritizing marriage and children themselves, our male respondents overwhelmingly assumed other men prioritized career success.

This is not just a male misperception issue. Women also overestimated the extent to which men prioritize their careers. Seventy-three percent of female respondents said they thought career success was more important to a majority of men than marriage and children, well above what men self-report.

Unsurprisingly, many male respondents also seemed to overestimate how many people agreed with the statement “men should be the breadwinners.” A plurality, 44%, thought the majority of Americans held this belief, while a plurality of female respondents, 46%, felt the opposite. In reality, the share of support among both men and women was much lower, at around 34% and 30%, respectively.

Subscribe now

As in our February poll, there is little evidence in our survey data to suggest that men see traditional gender roles as more favorable than modern egalitarian ones. As Jerusalem Demsas recently pointed out, strong baseline support for gender equality is an underrated fact of our modern political landscape: Around 81% of both male and female respondents agreed that women are equally suited to leadership. Among male respondents who voted for Donald Trump, the share was lower but still 72%.

The family-first MAGA breadwinner

Of course, being a man who values family over career is not the same as being a committed feminist. It is possible to think family is important and also want to reinstitute traditional gender roles. In fact, that seems to be more or less the prescription of today’s conservative thought leaders: Men should care about marriage and family, but they should behave as 1950s breadwinners.

The modern MAGA marriage of “pro-family” policy and masculinist ideals finds some support in our poll. Male Trump voters were considerably more likely to prioritize marriage and children over their careers than male Kamala Harris voters — 57% compared to 33%. They were also much more likely to agree with the statement “men should be the breadwinners,” with 51% endorsing the statement compared to just 15% of their Harris-voting peers.1

In itself, conservative men prioritizing family over career in a survey is not that surprising. What is striking is the gap between these men’s self-reported preference and what they assumed about other men. While over half of male Trump voters said getting married and having children was more important to them than career success, just 24% said this was true of most men.

In other words, conservative men want something for themselves that they think is at odds with what the majority of men want.

There has never been a better time to be a father

The reality is that most people would probably like to have fulfilling family lives as well as meaningful careers.

Having both was very difficult for American women until the late 20th century. Marriage bars — employer policies that barred married women from being hired or retained — were common through the early 1900s. But women’s labor force participation rose from around 40% in the mid-1960s to above 55% just two decades later.

Men also gained something tangible in the family realm over the same period. It is now common — and socially accepted — for fathers to be present during childbirth, push strollers in public, and pick their kids up from school. For children born as late as 1993, 77% of fathers didn’t take a single day of leave after their child was born. For children born between 2014 and 2022, that was true of only 35% of fathers.

The gap in the amount of time American men and women spend with their children has been narrowing for decades. Gen X fathers spent more than twice as much time with their kids as their predecessors did at the same age. Many found this time in part by cutting back daily hours at work.

Prominent voices on the right blame liberalism for rupturing the American family. They argue that its careerist individualism pushed Americans to marry later, have fewer children, and care more about money than anything else. Wilcox has dubbed this the “Midas Mindset,” the idea that “what matters most in your life is building your own individual brand, seeing work as the summit of your life, and steering clear of the encumbrances of family life.”

But to the extent that many men today can embrace being involved parents — who can opt out of the rat race in order to spend more time at home — it is largely thanks to the advances of the women who now contribute much more to household earnings than they used to.

In a world where men do not want to be breadwinners, women joining the labor force is a positive-sum game. If we take men at their word and assume that many of them would quite like to trade time at work for time at home, then discarding traditional gender roles is what makes that possible.

item.title: Who starts a political magazine?
item.content:encoded:
By Jerusalem Demsas

Welcome to The Closing Argument, our verdict on the news, plus everything The Argument published and appeared in this week.

The Verdict, by Jerusalem Demsas

Irving Howe, founding editor of Dissent, once quipped that “when intellectuals can do nothing else, they start a magazine.”

The founding of a political magazine is almost inevitably the result of a disaffected spirit. Those with power are too busy running the country and are likely satisfied with existing publications.

But if starting a magazine is a sign of discontent, it is simultaneously an act of hubris. The impulse to write manifestos and screeds, and to make the case for your ideological perspective, may only come to those who can observe the near-infinite amount of content being produced and decide still that they could do better.

The American Prospect openly embraced this impulse in its 1989 prospectus: “The natural reaction to any proposal for a new journal is that we are already swimming in a sea of words: Why more?”

My answer is the same as theirs: Because we are different.

The Prospect wasn’t the first magazine to make this claim,1 and The Argument won’t be the last. On the eve of this magazine’s anniversary, I went back to read the earliest issues of 20th-century political magazines. In the words of a junior writer at National Review: “Flushed with self-importance, we call attention to the fact that this is our First Anniversary issue and confess that we want to talk about it, or better, about ourselves, always an enjoyable way to pass the time.”

Some are more afraid of such overt self-aggrandizement and instead adopt a posture “at once modest and presumptuous,” in the words of Daniel Bell and Irving Kristol in the first issue of The Public Interest (which was something like the Vox of its day).2

Or take this from The New Republic’s opening issue in November 1914: “The New Republic is frankly an experiment.… Its success inevitably depends on public support, but if we are unable to achieve that success under the conditions essential to sound and disinterested thinking, we shall discontinue our experiment and make way for better men.”

That’s nice, but you’ll have to pry this magazine out of my cold, dead hands.

Libs athwart history

Despite founding a liberal publication myself, I recognized The Argument less in the modesty of The New Republic and The Public Interest than in the stridency of their conservative counterparts. It was while reading the latter that I saw my own frustration reflected back to me in biting prose.

Felix Morley, a Pulitzer Prize-winning journalist who left The Washington Post amid growing disagreement over U.S. intervention, co-founded Human Events in 1944. In the opening essay of the conservative anti-interventionist magazine’s first annual bound edition, Morley railed against “journalistic debasement” in coverage of international affairs, going so far as to compare it to Nazi propaganda: “While we have not yet carried these practices as far as did the unlamented Dr. Goebbels, the general direction of governmental propaganda has paid that Nazi leader the sincerest form of flattery.”

Other magazines on the right indulged in similar bluster. The famous one, of course, is National Review’s self-description as “standing athwart history, yelling stop.” Another is Reason magazine, launched in June 1968, which proclaimed: “We accept the responsibility that others have defaulted on. Others preferred to smear the issues with irrelevancies and falsifications. We don’t. Others preferred to be incomprehensible and incoherent. We don’t. Others preferred to ignore your mind. We won’t.”

The resemblance between these upstarts and The Argument is not ideological but positional: Magazines founded to advise a governing status quo can afford modesty, but magazines founded to help build a new paradigm cannot.

Liberalism was ascendant or hegemonic when America’s most significant liberal magazines were founded. The New Republic was started by men who sought to influence President Woodrow Wilson’s administration; The Public Interest was founded right after President Lyndon B. Johnson’s landslide victory and the triumph of civil rights legislation. While The American Prospect began publication in 1990 after three consecutive Republican presidential victories, small-l liberalism was still dominant: Democrats controlled Congress, the Cold War was coming to an end, and liberal democracy was on the rise around the world.

National Review, on the other hand, was founded as conservatism sought to claw its way back to relevance. The New Deal settlement had entrenched itself so thoroughly that, under the banner of what he called Modern Republicanism, President Dwight D. Eisenhower expanded Social Security, raised the federal minimum wage, and broadened unemployment-insurance coverage from within the GOP.

Reviewing these decades-old essays has also reminded me how far magazines can stray from their original purpose. Reason, once an Objectivist magazine, is now best characterized as libertarian; Commentary, once the flagship of liberal anti-Stalinism, is now a hawkish neoconservative outfit.

Part of what made The Argument necessary is that I found little of liberalism left in outlets like The American Prospect. In its 1989 prospectus, the latter called markets invaluable and defended the moniker “liberal” against attempts to rebrand as “progressive” or “populist”: “Denying the ‘liberal label’ suggests embarrassment and shame more than open-mindedness.” Now, the Prospect’s “about” page says it is devoted to the “progressive perspective.” Long gone is the magazine’s healthy respect for the market mechanism.3 Its editorial leadership is in the thrall to neo-Brandeisian economic populism and wouldn’t even take a clean stand against President Donald Trump’s illegal (and unpopular) tariffs.

It is a dark time for liberalism. The Trump administration has dispatched federal agents against law-abiding American citizens, lied brazenly to the courts, and begun dismantling the twin engines of progress: immigration and scientific research. Elite resistance to this assault on the American system is divided among left-wing populists with a tenuous relationship to basic tenets of liberty, centrist Democrats who lack any positive vision, and a dying breed of right-liberals.

Long liberalism

The Argument’s task is not to debate the policy agenda of an establishment that shares our commitments, but to make the case for a completely different paradigm. Things may seem dire, but I’m long liberalism:

  • No other ideology has been capable of delivering mass prosperity, economic growth, and scientific progress while protecting and expanding civil rights.

  • Despite decades of elite hostility to markets, capped off by Trump’s tariff regime, Americans remain committed to key tenets of economic liberalism and its promise of abundance.

  • In defiance of efforts to divide us by race, religion, and origin, Americans continue to believe that rights belong to individuals, that the law should treat us as equals, and that anyone can become fully and equally American.

While there are many individual liberals scattered throughout the great magazines and newspapers of this country, none of those publications offers a clear institutional voice willing to engage in the type of ideological combat necessary to rebuild American liberalism.

One thing I share with all the great political magazine founders, from the socialist dissenters to the Ayn Rand obsessives, is a belief in the power of ideas.

Howe, the Dissent editor whose line about intellectuals starting a magazine is oft-quoted, had more to say. In the very next sentence, he adds: “But starting a magazine is also doing something: at the very least it is thinking in common. And thinking in common can have unforeseen results.”4

The Argument is a bet on readers like you: ones who believe in a vision of liberalism abandoned by the current factions in American politics, who treasure rigorous, public debate as a tool for advancing the best ideas, and who are excited to be a part of a community as varied as this one. In the years to come, we’re going to keep picking fights and running polls and publishing pathbreaking essays. Thanks for libbing out with us.

Top stories this week, by Kobe Yank-Jacobs

This coming week marks one year since the launch of The Argument. To celebrate the occasion, we’ve launched an essay series on the question at the heart of political liberalism: How do we live with each other? In the coming weeks, you’ll get to see writers like Derek Thompson and Dylan Matthews wrestle with what we owe to people we disagree with in a liberal society, looking at the theme through a wide set of issues.

This week, Cassie Pritchard got us off to a strong start. She argues trans rights supporters need to stop arguing about whether trans women are women and focus instead on civil rights:

Economic historian Phil Magness followed this up with a rigorous case against JD Vance’s economics — or, rather, against Vance’s total ignorance of the field. Vance dedicates a whole chapter of his latest book to arguing that metrics like GDP distort our values, but he bases his gripes on absurd misunderstandings and nearly farcical anecdotes. Click to watch Magness lay a blow to the heart of MAGA economics:

Finally, while we answer the weighty questions at the heart of liberalism, we also continue to duke it out in the daily news cycle. This week, Jeremiah Johnson had some strong thoughts about the Hank Green AI-use controversy. To him, the most interesting thing about the episode isn’t the misuse of AI. It’s how wildly dogmatic Green’s science-minded fan base has become:

🌟Abundance wins of the week🌟

  • Bellingham, Washington, eliminated parking minimums, allowing developers to decide how many spaces new projects need while, of course, lowering construction costs.

  • In Connecticut, Eli Sabin beat a 21-term incumbent in the primary for a seat in the state legislature. Sabin was a leading advocate to upzone New Haven and may get to pick up his efforts in the state House should he notch a win in the general.

  • The FDA gave accelerated approval to a cancer drug for treatment-resistant advanced melanoma.

Share

Worth watching…

In recent decades, we’ve faced many crises of social connection: the loneliness epidemic, the deaths-of-despair phenomenon, the effects of phones on teens. But before all these, the source text for civic atrophy was Robert Putnam’s Bowling Alone, which documented a decline in U.S. associational life. No more bowling leagues, no more Rotary Clubs. Our chief malady, Putnam argued, was a decline in “social capital.”

Jerusalem is skeptical. This week on the pod, Jerusalem and Matt reassess one of the foundational texts of the 21st century and argue about how relevant it is to our current afflictions. Click below to see how it holds up:

Lakshya Jain hosted Rep. Kristen McDonald Rivet from Michigan’s 8th District. In their discussion, she shared some tricks of the trade. First, she emphasized how different primary and general electorates are. But the tip that hooked me was this one: She has a burner phone so she can escape the algorithm and listen to people outside of her ideological lane.

What’s News with The Argument

The Argument recommends, by Kobe Yank-Jacobs

Politicians never change their minds. They “evolve” on the issues. But here at The Argument, sometimes — just sometimes — we do change our minds. In fact, we even grow as people. New things appeal to us, old passions fade out.

That’s what I wanted to capture in this week’s recommendations section.

I asked the team to share media with social commentary that they used to agree with, and immediately, our social media director, Megha Fernandes, nailed it on my highly specific request:

This is a painting known as The Singing Butler by Jack Vettriano. So, um, what’s the social commentary here? you might ask. At first, Megha saw none either.

“To me, it was a beautiful depiction of being so in love that nothing else mattered,” she said. “The couple at the center didn’t even seem to notice the rain since they were too caught up in dancing together.”

But when she returned to her parents’ house as an adult, where a print hangs on the wall, she saw it differently. This was “class warfare,” she asserted over drinks at a team hangout the other night.

“Were they paid fairly? Did they even want to be out there?” she asked of the butler and the maid. “Suddenly, it seemed a lot easier for the couple to dance carefree in the rain when someone else was standing by, waiting with an umbrella.”

What I loved about Megha’s take was how closely she was reading the image. It prompted other teammates to take a second look at works they used to find meaning in.

It brought Jerusalem Demsas back to her own teenage radicalism. The social commentary she renounced? “Baby, I’m an Anarchist” by Against Me. For the record, she still thinks it’s a great song but declines to endorse the message.

“I no longer stand behind teenage Jerusalem's disdain for people who wouldn't throw rocks through Starbucks windows or hurl Molotov cocktails.”

God bless the parents of all teenagers.

Milan Singh followed this with an influential teenage experience of his own. He read The Omnivore’s Dilemma by Michael Pollan and became a vegetarian for five years. In his case, he doesn’t renounce the decision. In fact, he wishes he could stick with it. It’s just that, when he got to college, he found it hard to put on muscle on his ethical diet.

For my part? I actually had a few items in consideration, but the question to the team was motivated by a joyous car ride I spent relistening to Father John Misty’s 2017 album Pure Comedy. This is perhaps among the most wry and timely albums of social commentary I can imagine. It skewers the social media age in songs like “Total Entertainment Forever,” which closes:

When the historians find us we’ll be in our homes /
plugged into our hubs /
skin and bones, /
a frozen smile on every face /
as the stories replay /
This must have been a wonderful place

At the time, I was a self-branded Luddite, refusing as many conveniences of phones as I could manage while maintaining a college social life. Almost a decade later, it’s not so much that I disagree as that I’m resigned. I look back on my fickle resistance and finally understand Misty’s tone.

It’s ironic, in part, because in every song, his knowing speaker also participates in the shallow society he dismisses. He has to. How else can you be a good critic? So far away from the thing you critique?

As the team concluded our chat, weaving in and out of old anecdotes, I started to appreciate how much people treasured the items they’d stepped away from. It reminded me of a line from a Simon & Garfunkel song.5 “After changes upon changes we are more or less the same. / After changes, we are more or less the same.”

Only the incurably adolescent mind will find this fact of life distressing. Unfortunately, there are always more adolescent minds than adolescents around.”

See the Prospect‘s prospectus, which directly calls market mechanisms “invaluable,” treats markets and democratic politics as complementary, and acknowledges that liberals in another context might favor “greater reliance on market forces.”

See also Arthur Schlesinger Jr.’s opening salvo for the Prospect: “The liberal answers of the past were not infallible. Affirmative government sometimes tried to do too much. Regulations became intrusive and burdensome. Government programs miscarried. And the public interest, liberals must understand, is something more than, and very often different from, the sum of the interests of organized groups in our society.”

See also Cass Sunstein’s 1990 piece calling the private market “usually an engine of individual freedom and economic welfare.”
